The front end forwarded the attacker-routed request using the Exchange server's own Kerberos identity, which the back end trusted
The attacker used request smuggling
explain: The front end lent its own credentials to a request whose destination the attacker chose: SSRF with a confused deputy. The fix validated the routing value as a host name and stopped the front end from authenticating such requests as itself.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Inside the server: three processes and an overlapped loop
question: Why can't the scheduler simply build batch k+1 while batch k runs, with no extra machinery?
options: Batch k+1 needs batch k's sampled tokens as its inputs, which are not known until batch k finishes; SGLang uses future-token placeholders resolved on the GPU
The GPU cannot run two kernels in a row
Python cannot start a second thread
The radix tree must be rebuilt from scratch every step
explain: For decoding, each step's input is the previous step's output. Overlap therefore needs a way to refer to tokens that do not exist yet. The release notes describe resolving this dependency with future tokens and careful CUDA event synchronization.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: A*: steering the search with a lower bound
question: To speed things up, someone divides straight-line km by 30 km/h instead of the network's top speed of 60 km/h. What is the risk?
options: None; any distance-based estimate keeps A* optimal
A* will settle more nodes than before
The heuristic may now overestimate on fast roads, so A* can return a slower route than the optimum
The algorithm may loop forever
explain: At 30 km/h each kilometer is estimated at 2 minutes, but a 60 km/h road covers it in 1. Overestimating breaks Theorem 1's condition, so optimality is no longer guaranteed. The survey notes such aggressive bounds speed things up only by giving up correctness.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: Frequency bins, resolution and spectral leakage
question: You record 2 s of data at 1000 Hz and need to tell apart tones at 50.0 Hz and 50.3 Hz. What helps?
options: Zero-pad to 8 times the length before the FFT
Sample at 4000 Hz instead of 1000 Hz for the same 2 s
Record for longer: at least several seconds, since the bin spacing is 1/duration
Apply a Hann window, which sharpens peaks
explain: Resolution is fs/N = 1/duration. Two seconds gives 0.5 Hz bins, too coarse for a 0.3 Hz gap; you need more than 1/0.3 = 3.3 s, and more still with a window, which widens peaks. A higher fs adds bins at high frequencies but keeps the spacing at 1/duration. Zero-padding only interpolates the same blurred spectrum.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Writing a vector loop: intrinsics, reductions and tails
question: You remove the scalar tail loop from sum_avx2 to save code. What happens for n = 19?
options: Nothing, the vector loop reads all 19 elements
It returns 136, silently dropping a[16], a[17] and a[18]
It crashes because the last load is out of bounds
It returns 190 but more slowly
explain: The vector loop stops at i = 16 because 16 + 8 > 19, so it never reads past the end. Without the tail the last 3 elements are never added: you get 136 instead of 190. Silent wrong answers like this are the classic SIMD bug.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Shipping SIMD: -march levels, runtime dispatch, portability
question: You ship a desktop app built with `-march=x86-64-v4` because benchmarks on your AVX-512 workstation looked great. Users with AVX2-only laptops report crashes at startup. What is the right fix?
options: Add -O3
Build for the baseline or x86-64-v3 and use target_clones or runtime checks for the AVX-512 hot loops
Switch to -ffast-math
Catch SIGILL and retry
explain: x86-64-v4 lets the compiler place AVX-512 instructions anywhere, including startup code. Build the bulk for a level every user has, and multiversion only the hot kernels so each CPU picks its best copy.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: The slab allocator: caches of ready-made objects
question: A slab holds 31 objects of 128 bytes in a 4096-byte page, with 32 bytes of in-page metadata. Without coloring, every slab's objects start at offset 0. What does coloring change?
options: It fits a 32nd object into the page by moving the metadata elsewhere
It uses the 96 leftover bytes to start each new slab's objects at a different offset, so hot fields of objects in different slabs map to different cache sets
It rounds the objects up to 256 bytes so each one is cache-line aligned
It marks freed objects with a pattern so use-after-free is detected
explain: 31 x 128 = 3968 bytes, plus 32 metadata leaves 96 spare bytes. Coloring spends that otherwise wasted space on an offset that varies per slab. (Filling freed memory with 0xdeadbeef is a separate debugging feature.)

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Moving weights from Megatron into SGLang
question: You move a working colocated job to separate pools and add `--update-weight-mode delta` but keep the default transport. What happens?
options: It fails at startup: delta mode requires `--update-weight-transport disk`
It runs, shipping deltas over NCCL
It silently falls back to full NCCL sync
It uses CUDA IPC because the engines are on the same nodes
explain: Argument validation rejects it at startup, and `create_weight_updater` asserts the same: delta mode needs disk transport and no colocation. Delta sync works by publishing versioned checkpoint directories that engines pull, not by broadcasting.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Train-rollout mismatch in slime: TIS, IcePop, R3 and score centering
question: An FP8-rollout run on an MoE model shows `tis_clipfrac` climbing from 0.002 to 0.1 over a few hundred rollouts while reward stalls. Following slime's guidance, which change comes first?
options: Raise --tis-clip to 20 so fewer tokens are clipped
Switch to --use-rollout-logprobs to skip the trainer recompute
Enable --use-rollout-routing-replay to remove routing flips at the source, keep TIS, and compare clipfrac and log-prob gap with that single change
Turn TIS off, since clipping shows it is not working
explain: On an MoE model a large share of the gap comes from expert selection, which R3 removes; it is independent of TIS. Widening the clip only lets outliers through, bypassing the recompute removes the correction (slime even refuses it with `--use-tis` under the PPO loss), and turning TIS off leaves the gap uncorrected. Change one mechanism at a time and watch the metrics.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: The alert lifecycle, and why the queue is not first come, first served
question: Why does NIST advise against first-come, first-served handling?
options: Because older alerts are usually false positives
Because analysts work faster on new alerts
Because resources are limited and the order of work should follow risk: asset criticality, impact, how far the attack has progressed
Because SIEMs sort alerts randomly
explain: Ordering by arrival time lets the noisiest source decide what gets looked at. NIST lists risk evaluation factors such as asset criticality, functional and data impact, stage of observed activity and recoverability as the basis for triage and prioritisation.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: When the attacker calls the help desk: MFA resets and new devices
question: Why did the SolarWinds discovery start from a *routine* alert?
options: Because high-severity alerts were switched off
Because a careful analyst checked an MFA enrollment alert against what they knew about the user (location, existing devices, simultaneous sessions) and found contradictions
Because the backdoor itself raised the alert
Because the employee reported the phone
explain: Per Wired and NPR, the alert only said a new phone was enrolled. The analyst noticed it had no phone number, signed in from a state the employee did not live in, and was active at the same time as the employee's real phone, then called the employee. Context, not severity, made it matter.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Pivoting, building a timeline, and mapping it to ATT&CK
question: A firewall logs in local time without an offset (the appliance is set to UTC-05:00), and your EDR logs in UTC. A firewall line says 04:10 and an EDR line says 09:05. In UTC, which happened first?
options: The firewall event, at 04:10 UTC
They happened at the same moment
The EDR event: the firewall's 04:10 is 09:10 UTC, five minutes after the EDR's 09:05
It cannot be determined from timestamps
explain: Local 04:10 at UTC-05:00 is 09:10 UTC, five minutes after the EDR event. Ordering raw strings from mixed zones would have put the firewall event five hours earlier.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Metrics, burnout and the analyst's ethics
question: Your SOC's MTTA improved from 20 to 6 minutes after a new rule let analysts bulk-close alerts from noisy rules. What should you check before celebrating?
options: Nothing; faster is better
Whether true positives are still being found and how fast they were acknowledged, and whether bulk closures carry reasons that quality review can check
Whether the analysts are working longer hours
Whether the SIEM clock is correct
explain: Speed can improve by doing less looking. The metric that matters is how quickly real attacks were caught, and whether closures are still evidence-based. That is the gaming risk the SOUPS study describes.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Password and MFA friction: rules that backfire and rules that work
question: Under NIST SP 800-63B-4, which policy is allowed for a password used as a single factor?
options: Minimum 15 characters, checked against a blocklist, no composition rules
Minimum 8 characters, must contain a digit and a symbol
Must be changed every 90 days
Must have a hint so users can recover it
explain: Single-factor passwords need at least 15 characters. Composition rules, periodic changes and hints are all prohibited by SHALL NOT statements in the guideline.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: The help desk as an attack surface: MGM, Okta's warning and Clorox
question: A help desk procedure requires 'manager name and username' before a reset. What is its main weakness?
options: It takes too long
It requires a manager to be online
Both facts are often discoverable from public profiles, org charts or earlier calls, so they do not prove identity
Usernames are secret by design
explain: Mandiant's hardening guide warns against relying on publicly available personal data because the group 'often possesses this information'. Proof must be something the attacker cannot research or buy.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: What a lock really does: pin tumblers, master keys and key control
question: Why does Blaze's finding matter more for an office tower with tenants than for a single-family house?
options: Tower locks are cheaper
Houses have no locks
Many unrelated people hold change keys in the same master system, so one of them could amplify their access to all doors
Towers have more windows
explain: The attack starts from a legitimate change key and its lock. A large master-keyed system hands that starting point to many people, any of whom could derive the master.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: A reporting culture, and what to do when someone is fooled
question: An employee admits they approved an MFA prompt they did not start, two hours ago. What should the first response be?
options: Schedule them for mandatory retraining before anything else
Wait to see whether anything bad happens
Reset only their password
Thank them, revoke their sessions, re-secure their factors and check what the session did
explain: The stolen session, not the password, is the attacker's access, so sessions must be revoked and factors checked. Thanking them keeps reporting alive; retraining first signals blame.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Enforcing sparsity: L1, TopK and JumpReLU
question: An L1 SAE's latents look right on inspection, but its reconstructions are consistently a bit too short (smaller norm than x). What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: Dead latents; resample them
The learning rate is too high; lower it
Shrinkage from the L1 penalty; use TopK, JumpReLU or a Gated SAE, or re-fit magnitudes on the chosen latents
The dictionary is too large; reduce M
explain: L1 pulls every active magnitude down by about lambda/2 (in the one-latent case), so x-hat is systematically small. Architectures that decouple selection from magnitude remove this bias.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Measuring an SAE and steering a model with its features
question: You clamp a latent to a large negative value although the encoder never outputs negatives. What happens to the activation?
options: Nothing; negative clamps are clipped to zero
A negative multiple of the latent's decoder direction is added to x
The latent's decoder direction is deleted
All other latents are set to zero
explain: Scaling Monosemanticity notes that clamping to a negative value simply gives a negative multiple of the feature vector. In their code-error example, negative clamping made the model predict the output the code would have produced without the bug.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: The semivariogram: measuring how similarity decays with distance
question: Why fit a model like the spherical one instead of plugging the four empirical bin values directly into kriging?
options: The empirical values are in the wrong units
Kriging needs semivariance at arbitrary distances, and the model must be a valid one so that every predicted variance is non-negative
Spherical models always fit better than the empirical values
Fitting removes the need to choose a nugget
explain: Kriging asks for $\gamma$ at every sensor-to-sensor and sensor-to-target distance, not just the bin centers, and arbitrary numbers can produce negative variances. Valid model families avoid that.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Draft, verify, keep: the loop with greedy decoding
question: A round with gamma = 5 finds the first mismatch at guess 4 (1-based). How many tokens does it append?
explain: Guesses 1 to 3 are accepted and the target's own token replaces guess 4, giving 4 tokens. Guess 5 and the bonus slot are discarded because they were computed after a rejected token.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Drafting without a second model: Medusa heads and token trees
question: With s1 = 3, s2 = 2, s3 = 2, how many tree nodes must the target verify in one pass?
explain: Level sizes are 3, 3 x 2 = 6 and 3 x 2 x 2 = 12, for 3 + 6 + 12 = 21 nodes. Twelve full candidate paths share their prefixes, which is why tree attention is cheaper than 12 separate sequences of length 3.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Self-speculation: MTP heads, layer skipping and lookahead
question: A team drafts with the first 16 of 32 layers of an off-the-shelf model, with no retraining, and sees almost no accepted tokens. What is the most likely reason?
options: The LM head was trained to read only the last layer's output, so early hidden states give poor predictions
Early layers cannot use the KV cache
The verify pass must also stop at layer 16
Greedy decoding cannot be used with layer skipping
explain: On SmolLM2-360M an exit after 16 of 32 layers matched the full model on 13% of tokens. LayerSkip adds an early exit loss so the shared LM head learns to read earlier layers.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Word error rate: alignments, normalization and fair comparisons
question: Your new model lowers WER on your test set from 9% to 6%, but you also switched to a normalizer that expands numbers and removes filler words. What should you conclude?
options: The model is 33% better
Nothing yet: rescore the old model with the new normalizer and compare
The old normalizer was wrong, so only the new number counts
WER is meaningless and should be replaced by human judgment
explain: Two things changed at once. The Whisper paper reports normalization alone moving WER by up to 50% on some datasets. Score both models with the same normalizer before attributing the gain to the model.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Walking an x86-64 page table, bit by bit
question: For virtual address 0x00007f3a12345678 mapped with a 2 MiB huge page, which bits form the offset within the page?
options: Bits 11 to 0
Bits 20 to 0
Bits 29 to 0
Bits 47 to 21
explain: A 2 MiB page is $2^{21}$ bytes, so the offset is the low 21 bits (here 0x145678). The PMD entry maps the page directly, so bits 20 to 12, which would normally index a PTE table, become part of the offset.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: When RAM runs out: page cache, file mappings, swap and thrashing
question: With $T_M$ = 100 ns and $T_D$ = 10 ms, roughly what average access time does a 1 percent page-fault rate give?
options: About 100 microseconds, 1,000 times slower than RAM
About 1 microsecond
About 10 milliseconds
About 200 nanoseconds
explain: AMAT = 100 ns + 0.01 x 10 ms = 100 ns + 100 microseconds, about 100.1 microseconds, roughly 1,000 times the 100 ns memory cost. Ten times the miss rate of OSTEP's 0.1 percent example gives ten times the slowdown.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Side effects and how to evaluate a steering vector
question: A team builds a sycophancy vector from 500 A/B pairs, picks the layer and coefficient that maximize the score on those same 500 pairs, and reports a large effect. What is the main flaw?
options: They should have used fewer pairs
Sycophancy cannot be represented linearly
They should have reported MMLU instead of the behavior score
The vector, the hyperparameters and the reported score all come from the same data, so the effect is likely overstated; it needs held-out validation and test splits
explain: Choosing layer and c on the evaluation data overfits them to it. CAA scores on 50 held-out questions, ITI uses 2-fold cross-validation, and Arditi et al. keep train, validation and evaluation sets pairwise disjoint. Capability checks are needed too, but they do not fix the leak.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Beyond one fixed vector: conditional, learned and monitoring uses
question: What is the main cost BiPO and LoReFT pay compared with a difference-of-means vector?
options: They change all the model's weights
They cannot be applied at inference time
They need labelled or preference data and gradient-based training through the frozen model
They only work on models under 1 billion parameters
explain: Both keep the model's weights frozen and train only the intervention (a vector for BiPO, R, W and b for LoReFT), which requires backpropagation and suitable data. Difference of means needs only forward passes on contrast pairs.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Downsampling, retention and exactly-once vs at-least-once
question: Your sink appends one row per window firing. With allowed lateness 5 s, window [0,10) fires at count 4 and later at count 5. A dashboard sums all rows per window. What goes wrong and what fixes it?
options: The window is counted as 4 + 5 = 9 readings; write with an upsert keyed by (sensor, window) since firings are accumulating
Nothing; the second firing contains only the late reading
Late firings are never sent to sinks
The fix is to set allowed lateness higher
explain: In accumulating mode each firing is the full refined result, so appending both rows double counts. Overwrite by window key, or use discarding mode and have the consumer add deltas, or emit retractions.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Causal masks, teacher forcing and cross-attention
question: A bug report: a decoder trains to near-zero loss quickly, but generates garbage at inference. Which bug is most likely?
options: The scale factor uses d_model instead of d_k
The causal mask is missing, so during training each position could read the token it was supposed to predict
The model uses 8 heads instead of 1
The softmax is applied over columns instead of rows
explain: With teacher forcing the whole target is fed in at once. Without the causal mask, position i can attend to position i+1 (its own answer), so training is trivially easy. At inference those future tokens do not exist yet, and the model has never learned to predict without them.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: One layer end to end, in numbers and in code, and how it decodes
question: Which statement about beam search with beam size B = 1 is correct?
options: It is the same as greedy decoding: only the single best partial output is kept each step
It explores every possible sentence, so it always finds the most probable one
It needs teacher forcing at inference
It is the paper's setting for the base model
explain: Keeping one hypothesis and extending it by its most probable token is exactly greedy decoding. No practical beam search explores every sentence; the paper used B = 4. Teacher forcing applies only to training.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Document length normalization: what b controls
question: Your index holds tweets whose lengths all fall between 25 and 35 tokens, and nothing else. You move b from 0.75 to 0.3. What do you expect?
options: Large ranking changes, because tweets vary in length
All scores become zero
Scores become probabilities
Small changes, because lengths are all close to avgdl so B stays near 1 either way
explain: B = (1 - b) + b x |d|/avgdl. When every |d|/avgdl is near 1, B is near 1 for any b, so b has little effect. b matters most when lengths vary a lot.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Stacking blocks: residuals, pre-LayerNorm, MLP and a tied output head
question: In nanoGPT's Block, where is LayerNorm applied?
options: After each residual addition, x = LN(x + attn(x))
On the input to each sub-layer, x = x + attn(LN(x)), plus one final ln_f
Only once, before the first block
Only on the attention scores before the softmax
explain: GPT-2 moved LayerNorm to the input of each sub-block and added a final LayerNorm after the last block. The first option is the post-LN layout of the 2017 Transformer.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: The training loop end to end: data, evals, overfitting, checkpoints
question: Why does nanoGPT store OpenWebText as uint16 and not int64 like the tensors it trains on?
options: Every GPT-2 token id is at most 50,256, which fits in 16 bits, so the 9-billion-token file is 4 times smaller; get_batch converts each slice to int64
uint16 makes the tokenizer faster
PyTorch embeddings require 16-bit indices
Negative ids mark document boundaries
explain: Two bytes per token gives the 17 GB train.bin; int64 would be 72 GB. The conversion to int64 happens only for the few slices that get_batch reads. End-of-text is the ordinary id 50256, not a negative number.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Derivative rules and the chain rule for nested functions
question: Someone computes $\frac{d}{dx}\ln(x^2 + 1)$ at $x = 1$ and gets $1/2$. What went wrong?
options: Nothing; 1/2 is correct
They used 1/u with u = 2 but forgot to multiply by du/dx = 2x = 2; the answer is 1
They should have used 1/x, giving 1
The log has no derivative at 1
explain: Outer: $d\ln(u)/du = 1/u = 1/2$ at $u = 2$. Inner: $du/dx = 2x = 2$. The chain rule multiplies them: $1/2 \times 2 = 1$. Forgetting the inner factor is the most common chain-rule error.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Gradient descent: walking downhill and choosing the step size
question: Two losses are $x^2 + 3y^2$ and $x^2 + 30y^2$. Compared with the first, what happens to the largest stable learning rate for plain gradient descent on the second?
options: It stays 1/3 because the x term is unchanged
It increases, because the bowl is steeper so it is easier to find the bottom
It drops to 1/30, because the steepest direction now has a = 30
It is unlimited, because the minimum is still at the origin
explain: Using the factor $1 - 2a\eta$, the $30y^2$ term needs $\eta < 1/30$. The steepest direction caps the step size for all parameters, so the shallow $x$ direction now crawls. This mismatch is called poor conditioning.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: What happens when you press Enter: lookup, fork, exec, wait
question: A script `setup.sh` contains `cd build` and `export MODE=dev`. You run it as `./setup.sh`, then type `pwd`. What do you see?
options: Your original directory, and MODE is unset in your shell
The build directory, because the script changed into it
The build directory, but MODE is unset because export only affects children
An error, because cd is a builtin and cannot run in a script
explain: `./setup.sh` runs in a child bash process. Its cd and export change only that child, which then exits. To apply them to your current shell you must run the file inside it with `source setup.sh` (or `. setup.sh`).

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Pipes: concurrent processes, sort | uniq -c, and SIGPIPE
question: `grep ERROR huge.log | head -n 5` returns almost instantly even though huge.log is 50 GB. Why?
options: grep detects the head command and reads only 5 lines
head reads the file directly and grep is skipped
The kernel caches the whole file before grep starts
Once head exits after 5 lines, grep's next write raises SIGPIPE and grep dies
explain: Both run concurrently. After head has its five lines it exits, closing the read end. grep's next write to the pipe triggers SIGPIPE, ending it long before it reaches the end of the file.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Your environment and remote machines: dotfiles, ssh and tmux
question: Your public key is in the server's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, yet ssh falls back to asking for a password. On the server, `ls -ld ~/.ssh` shows `drwxrwxrwx`. What is the likely cause?
options: sshd will not use authorized_keys while ~/.ssh is writable by other users
The key type is wrong for this server
known_hosts on your laptop is missing
The private key must also be copied to the server
explain: Anyone who can write to `~/.ssh` could add their own key, so sshd refuses to trust authorized_keys there (its StrictModes check). `chmod 700 ~/.ssh` and `chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys` fix it. The private key must never be copied to the server.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Train word2vec yourself: SGNS in PyTorch, then gensim
question: You change the PyTorch script to `torch.optim.Adam([v.weight, u.weight])` and keep `sparse=True`. What happens?
options: Training runs normally but uses more memory
Adam silently ignores the embedding rows
The first `opt.step()` raises an error, because Adam does not accept sparse gradients
Adam converts the gradients to dense and trains the same model
explain: PyTorch raises `RuntimeError: Adam does not support sparse gradients, please consider SparseAdam instead`. Either keep `sparse=True` with SparseAdam (or SGD), or drop `sparse=True` and use dense Adam, which then updates moment estimates for every row on every step.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Where word vectors fail: unseen words, many senses and bias
question: Your fastText model gives the unseen word *unhappiness* a vector close to *happiness* and *sadness*. Which part of the model made that possible?
options: The context vectors of the words around *unhappiness* at query time
A shared unknown-word row
The n-gram vectors it shares with seen words, such as *hap*, *ness* and *ness>*, summed into a vector
The full softmax over the vocabulary
explain: An unseen word has no word vector, but its character n-grams were trained inside other words. fastText sums their vectors. At query time there is no context and no training, and an unknown row would give every unseen word the same vector.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Inside a GPU: many small cores fed by one big memory
question: Why does the GPU keep many warps resident on each SM?
options: So that while some warps wait for memory, others can execute math
Because each warp can only run one instruction in its lifetime
To increase the size of HBM
Because warps of 32 threads cannot share an SM
explain: GPUs hide dependent instruction and memory latency by switching to other ready warps. That is why the number of threads needed is much larger than the number of execution units.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: The KV cache: why memory grows with every token
question: A server runs LLaMA-7B in FP16 on an 80 GB A100 with 2048-token contexts. Ignoring overheads, roughly how many full sequences fit in the KV space?
options: About 31
About 2,048
About 62
Unlimited, KV lives in host memory
explain: Each sequence needs 2048 x 512 KiB = 1 GiB (about 1.07 GB). 66.6 GB / 1.07 GB is about 62. Halving the context doubles how many fit.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Bits, bytes and hex: how numbers are stored
question: What range of values fits in a signed 8-bit integer (two's complement)?
explain: The top bit weighs -128, so the smallest value is 1000 0000 = -128 and the largest is 0111 1111 = 127. There is one more negative value than positive ones because 0 uses a pattern with the top bit clear. 0 to 255 is the unsigned range of the same 8 bits.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Why real CPUs beat the simple loop: pipelines and prediction
question: An ideal five-stage pipeline (no stalls, no mispredictions) runs 100 instructions. How many cycles does it take?
explain: The first instruction needs 5 cycles to get through all five stages, and after that one more instruction finishes every cycle: 5 + 99 = 104. 500 is the unpipelined time; exactly 100 would ignore the cycles needed to fill the pipeline.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Pretraining: next-token loss over trillions of tokens
question: A model with a 50,000-token vocabulary predicts the uniform distribution at every position. What is its average cross-entropy loss?
options: 0 nats, because it never assigns zero probability
About 0.69 nats, which is ln(2)
About 10.8 nats, which is ln(50,000)
50,000 nats
explain: Uniform means p(target) = 1/50,000 everywhere, so the loss is -ln(1/50,000) = ln(50,000), about 10.82 nats. Real training starts near this value and falls as the model learns.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Where preference data comes from: guidelines, safety, AI feedback
question: Three of four labelers prefer A over B for some pair. With enough such data, what reward gap does a Bradley-Terry reward model converge to for this pair?
options: A gap that grows without limit, because A always wins on average
0, because the labelers disagree
Exactly 0.75, the fraction of labelers
About ln 3 = 1.10, so that sigmoid of the gap is 0.75
explain: The expected loss -(0.75 log sigma(d) + 0.25 log sigma(-d)) is minimized where sigma(d) = 0.75, so d = ln(0.75/0.25) = ln 3. Disagreement caps the gap and leaves a nonzero loss floor; it does not zero the reward or let it grow forever.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: From grep to the inverted index
question: Using the six documents, which documents match the Boolean query hot AND NOT deploy?
options: d1 and d4
d4 only
d1, d2, d4 and d5
No documents
explain: hot has postings d1, d4. deploy has postings d2, d3, d5, so NOT deploy is d1, d4, d6. The intersection is d1 and d4. Neither of them mentions deploy.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Ranking with vectors and cosine similarity
question: Using raw tf weights, you append a document to itself (every tf doubles, nothing else changes, and the document collection statistics stay the same). What happens to its cosine score for any query?
options: It doubles
It stays exactly the same
It increases by a factor of sqrt(2)
It drops, because the document is now longer
explain: With raw tf, every weight doubles, so the vector is scaled by 2. Scaling a vector does not change its direction, and cosine depends only on direction, so the score is unchanged. A plain TF-IDF sum would double, which is exactly the length bias cosine removes.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Multi-file C: headers, include guards, static, extern and make
question: util.c defines `static int helper(void) { ... }`. main.c declares `int helper(void);` and calls it. What happens?
options: It builds and runs, because the prototype matches
Compile error in util.c
Compile error in main.c, because helper is static
Link error: no definition of helper is visible to main.o
explain: Each file compiles: main.c only needs the declaration. But static gives util.c's helper internal linkage, so it is not exported to the linker, and main.o's reference to helper finds no definition. Clang on macOS reported `Undefined symbols ... "_helper", referenced from: _main in m.o`.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Object lifetimes: automatic, static and malloc'd memory
question: Which of these functions returns a pointer that the caller can safely use after the function returns?
options: int *f(void) { int n = 1; return &n; }
int *g(void) { int a[3] = {0}; return a; }
int *h(void) { int *p = malloc(sizeof *p); if (p) *p = 1; return p; }
All three, because the bytes are still in memory
explain: f and g return the address of automatic objects (g's array decays to a pointer to a[0]), whose lifetime ends at return. h returns allocated storage, which lives until free, so the caller may use it and is responsible for freeing it.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Undefined behavior, and the tools that catch it
question: Which of these operations has fully defined behavior in standard C?
options: int x = INT_MAX; x = x + 1;
unsigned u = UINT_MAX; u = u + 1;
int a[5]; int y = a[5];
free(p); free(p);
explain: Unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo 2 to the power of the bit width, so u becomes 0. Signed overflow, reading one past the end of an array, and freeing twice are all undefined behavior.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Who frees this memory? Ownership and drop
question: Three local variables `x`, `y`, `z` (declared in that order) all implement `Drop`. In what order do their `drop` methods run at the end of the block?
options: x, y, z
Unspecified; it depends on the optimizer
z, y, x
explain: Locals are dropped in reverse order of declaration, as specified in the Rust Reference. This is deterministic, not up to the optimizer.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Slices and why references cannot dangle
question: Why does returning `&s[0..5]` from `first_word` prevent the clear-then-use bug, when returning the index 5 did not?
options: Slices are copied, so clearing `s` does not affect them
The slice is a borrow of `s`, so any `&mut s` (like `clear`) while it is still used is a compile error
`clear` checks at run time whether slices exist
explain: The borrow checker tracks the slice as a shared borrow of `s`. `clear` needs a mutable borrow, and shared XOR mutable makes the overlap illegal. There is no run-time check involved.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A vector is a list of numbers and an arrow at the same time
question: An embedding $\mathbf{v} = [0.6, 0.8]$ is multiplied by the scalar $-2$. What happens to it as an arrow?
options: It points the opposite way and its length becomes 2
It rotates 90 degrees and keeps its length
It points the opposite way and its length becomes -2
It keeps its direction and its length becomes 2
explain: $-2\mathbf{v} = [-1.2, -1.6]$, whose norm is $\sqrt{1.44+2.56} = 2$. The minus sign flips the direction; lengths are never negative, so the length is $|{-2}| \times 1 = 2$. Scaling never rotates by anything other than 0 or 180 degrees.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Matrix multiplication: composing maps and checking shapes
question: You need $ABx$ where $A$ and $B$ are $1000 \times 1000$ and $x$ is a vector. Which order of evaluation is cheaper?
options: (AB)x, because multiplying matrices first is faster
A(Bx), because two matrix-vector products cost about 2 million multiply-adds versus about 1 billion for AB
They cost the same because multiplication is associative
Neither; you must invert A first
explain: Associativity guarantees the same answer, not the same cost. $AB$ alone is $1000^3 = 10^9$ multiply-adds. $B\mathbf{x}$ then $A(B\mathbf{x})$ is $2 \times 1000^2 = 2\times10^6$.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: The SVD: rotate, stretch, rotate, then keep what matters
question: PCA on centered 2D data gives singular values 9 and 3. What share of the variance does the first component capture?
options: 75 percent
90 percent
81 percent
97 percent
explain: Variance shares use squared singular values: $81/(81 + 9) = 0.9$. 75 percent comes from using $9/(9+3)$ without squaring.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Many features: linear regression in matrix form and feature scaling
question: $X$ has 500 rows (examples) and 20 columns (19 features plus the ones column). What is the shape of $\nabla L = \frac{2}{n}X^\top(Xw - y)$?
options: 500 by 1, one entry per example
20 by 20, like the Hessian
20 by 1, one partial derivative per weight
500 by 20, like X
explain: $Xw - y$ has one residual per example (500). $X^\top$ is 20 by 500, so the product has 20 entries: one partial derivative for each of the 20 weights, including the bias. The 20 by 20 matrix is $X^\top X$, which appears in the Hessian and the normal equations.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Validation and penalties: choosing lambda, L2 and L1
question: You fit a lasso on 200 features and 180 of the learned weights come out exactly 0. What is the most reasonable reading?
options: The solver failed to converge
The L1 penalty judged those 180 features not worth their cost, so the model uses only 20
L1 always zeroes 90 percent of the weights
The features must have been standardized wrongly
explain: Exact zeros are what L1 is for: its constant-size pull pins weak weights at 0, giving a sparse model that effectively selects 20 features. How many survive depends on alpha, chosen on validation data. L2 would have kept all 200 small but nonzero.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Data pitfalls: leakage, distribution shift and baselines
question: Before splitting, you fill missing values in a column with the mean of the whole dataset. Is that leakage?
options: No, means are harmless
Only if the column is the label
Yes: the fill value used held-out rows; compute it on the training fold only
Only for time series
explain: Imputation is a fitted preprocessing step like scaling. Its fill value should be learned from training rows and reused for validation and test. The effect is usually small for a mean, but the habit matters, and a Pipeline makes it automatic.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: The forward pass: layers as matrix multiplies
question: In the convention $z^l = W^l a^{l-1} + b^l$, what is the shape of $W^2$ for that 784-100-10 network?
explain: $W^l$ has one row per unit in layer $l$ and one column per unit in layer $l-1$: 10 output units by 100 hidden units.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: The cost of backprop: compute, activation memory, checkpointing
question: You double the batch size and the run now goes out of GPU memory, even though the model's weights are unchanged. What is the most likely cause?
options: The weights are copied once per example
Backprop needs a second copy of the loss
Stored activations for the backward pass scale with batch size
Gradients scale with batch size while weights do not, and gradients are the bulk
explain: Weights and their gradients have a fixed size. Activations kept for the backward pass scale with batch size times depth, so they grow. Remedies: a smaller batch, gradient checkpointing (recompute instead of store), or lower precision activations.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Processes and limited direct execution
question: Why must the instruction that installs the trap table be privileged?
options: Because it is slow and should run only at boot
Because the trap table is stored on disk
Because a user process could otherwise point system calls and interrupts at its own code and take over the machine
Because user programs do not know the system-call numbers
explain: The trap table decides which code runs in kernel mode on every trap and interrupt. If a user program could install its own, it would run arbitrary code with full privilege, defeating all protection. So, like starting the timer, it is restricted to kernel mode.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Concurrency: race conditions and locks
question: On a single CPU with a non-preemptive scheduler (no timer switches), Thread 2 calls a spin lock held by Thread 1. What happens?
options: Thread 2 acquires the lock after one time slice
Thread 2 spins forever: Thread 1 never gets the CPU back to release the lock
The lock automatically turns into a sleeping lock
Thread 1 releases the lock because spinning causes an interrupt
explain: A spinning thread never gives up the CPU on its own. Without preemption, the holder never runs again, so the lock is never released. OSTEP points out that spin locks need a preemptive scheduler to work correctly on a single processor.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Persistence: how a hard disk spends its time
question: Why can SSTF (shortest seek time first) starve a request?
options: Because it ignores rotation time
Because the OS does not know the disk's geometry
Because a steady stream of requests near the head always wins, so a request far away may never be served
Because it serves requests in arrival order
explain: SSTF always picks the closest request. If new nearby requests keep arriving, the far one is never closest. The elevator (SCAN) algorithm fixes this by sweeping in one direction, so every request is reached within a sweep. Ignoring rotation is a real weakness of both, but it is not the cause of starvation.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Probability by counting outcomes, and what conditioning does
question: A model's training set has 1,000 emails: 300 are spam, and 240 of the spam emails contain the word "free". Of the 700 non-spam emails, 70 contain "free". What is P(spam | contains "free")?
options: 0.80, because 240 of 300 spam emails contain free
0.24, because 240 of 1,000 emails are spam with free
About 0.77, because 240 of the 310 emails containing free are spam
0.30, the base rate of spam
explain: Condition on the event you observed: restrict to the 240 + 70 = 310 emails containing "free", of which 240 are spam, so 240/310 = 0.774. Option A is P(free | spam), the reverse conditional, a very common mix-up that the next lesson is about.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Continuous variables: densities, CDFs and common distributions
question: X is uniform on [0, 0.5]. Which statement is true?
options: Its density cannot exceed 1, so it is 1 on the interval
P(X = 0.25) = 2, the density there
Its density is 2 on the interval, and P(0.1 <= X <= 0.2) = 0.2
P(0.1 <= X <= 0.2) = 0.1, the length of the range
explain: The area must be 1 over a width of 0.5, so the height is 2. A range probability is width times height: 0.1 x 2 = 0.2. The length alone (0.1) is only right when the density is 1, and any single exact value has probability 0.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Entropy, cross-entropy and KL divergence
question: A language model's average cross-entropy on a test set is 2.0 nats per token. What is its perplexity?
options: About 7.4
About 0.14
explain: Perplexity is e to the cross-entropy in nats: e^2 = 7.39, as uncertain as choosing among about 7.4 equally likely tokens at each step. 4.0 would be 2 raised to 2.0, which is right only if the 2.0 were measured in bits.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Why loss falls on a straight line in log-log space
question: On log-log axes, a team's loss-versus-parameters points lie on a straight line with slope -0.07. Which statement is correct?
options: Each doubling of N removes the same fraction of the loss
Each doubling of N removes the same absolute amount of loss
Loss will reach zero at a finite model size
The slope says how much data the model needs
explain: A straight line in log-log space is a power law: equal multiplicative steps in N give equal multiplicative changes in L, here $2^{-0.07} \approx 0.95$ per doubling. Absolute drops shrink, the curve never reaches zero, and the slope says nothing about data needs on its own.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Kaplan vs Chinchilla: why 2020-era models were undertrained
question: GPT-3 used about 3.2e+23 FLOPs. Using $C \approx 6ND$ and Chinchilla's 20 tokens per parameter, what would a compute-optimal model at that budget look like?
options: 175B parameters on 300B tokens
About 500B parameters on 105B tokens
About 12B parameters on 4.3T tokens
About 51B parameters on 1.0T tokens
explain: Set $D = 20N$, so $C = 6 \cdot N \cdot 20N = 120N^2$ and $N = \sqrt{C/120} \approx 51$B, $D \approx 1.0$T. GPT-3's actual 175B on 300B tokens is the Kaplan-style choice; 12B on 4.3T overshoots the token ratio badly.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Precision, recall, and why accuracy is useless for search
question: A legal team must find every contract mentioning a clause before a court deadline, and a junior reviewer will read whatever is returned. Which metric should you optimize first?
options: Precision at 1
Recall (at a generous cutoff)
Accuracy over the whole collection
Precision at 10
explain: Missing a relevant contract is the costly error, and the team will read through extra results, so recall matters most. P@1 and P@10 measure only the top of the list, and accuracy is dominated by the huge number of true negatives.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: From token vectors to one sentence vector: pooling and cosine
question: Your service embeds documents in batches of 32. The same document gets clearly different vectors depending on which batch it lands in. What is the most likely bug?
options: The model is non-deterministic because of dropout at inference
Cosine similarity is unstable for vectors of length 1
Mean pooling is averaging over padding positions instead of using the attention mask
The tokenizer lowercases differently per batch
explain: Padding length depends on the longest text in the batch, so if pooling ignores the attention mask, the number and effect of [PAD] rows changes with batch composition. Dropout is disabled in eval mode, and tokenization does not depend on the batch.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Why language models read subwords, not words or characters
question: You double a model's vocabulary size, keeping everything else fixed. Which pair of effects should you expect?
options: Longer sequences and a smaller embedding table
No change in sequence length, only more parameters
Shorter token sequences for the same text, and a larger embedding table
Shorter sequences and fewer parameters
explain: More vocabulary entries let the tokenizer keep longer pieces, so the same text needs fewer tokens. But each new entry is another row of $d$ numbers in the embedding table (and in the output layer that predicts the next token).

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Build a byte-level BPE tokenizer in Python
question: A chat app streams replies by decoding each new token on its own with `bytes.decode("utf-8")`. English replies work; Japanese replies crash with UnicodeDecodeError. What is the bug?
options: A single token can hold only part of a multi-byte character, so decoding one token alone can be invalid UTF-8; buffer bytes until characters are complete
The tokenizer has no Japanese tokens, so it emits unknown ids
UTF-8 cannot represent Japanese characters
The encoder applied the merges in the wrong order
explain: Byte-level BPE can always encode Japanese (every byte is a token), but merges ignore character boundaries. In GPT-2, 日 is split across two tokens, and the first holds 2 of its 3 bytes. Decoding that alone with strict errors fails. Keep the bytes and decode once characters are complete, or decode with errors="replace".

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Initialization: keeping signals alive through 30 layers
question: A 50-layer ReLU MLP uses weights with $\mathrm{Var}(w) = 1/\text{fan-in}$. Without normalization layers, what do you expect at initialization?
options: Activations shrink by about a factor of 2 in variance per layer, so early-layer gradients become tiny
Activations keep roughly constant scale, since 1/fan-in is the textbook choice
Activations explode because ReLU outputs are always positive
Nothing depends on initialization because Adam rescales every step
explain: Var(w) = 1/n gives g = 1, so the variance factor per layer is g/2 = 1/2. After 50 layers the variance is multiplied by about $2^{-49}$. The backward pass has the same product, so early gradients vanish. Adam, the adaptive optimizer of lesson 3, rescales update sizes, but it cannot repair a forward pass whose signal has already disappeared.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Learning rate: the stability limit, warmup, decay and clipping
question: One step's gradients are 3 for layer A and 4 for layer B, and max_norm = 1. What does clip_grad_norm_ produce, and what would clip_grad_value_ with a limit of 1 produce?
options: (1, 1) for both: each caps every entry at 1
(0.75, 1) and (1, 1): norm clipping divides by the largest entry
(0.6, 0.8) and (1, 1): norm clipping keeps the direction, value clipping turns it
(0.6, 0.8) for both
explain: The global norm is sqrt(9 + 16) = 5, so clip_grad_norm_ multiplies everything by 1 / 5, giving (0.6, 0.8): norm 1, same direction. clip_grad_value_ clamps each entry to [-1, 1], giving (1, 1), which points at 45 degrees instead of 53 and gives A as much weight as B.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: A debugging recipe: loss at init, overfit one batch, read the curves
question: Training loss keeps falling, but after epoch 12 validation loss rises steadily. What is the recipe's next move?
options: Increase the learning rate to escape the minimum
Re-initialize with He init
Regularize: more data or augmentation, dropout, weight decay, or stop early at the best validation loss
Remove model.eval() so validation uses batch statistics
explain: Diverging train and validation curves are overfitting, which is exactly what stage 4 (regularize) addresses. Early stopping on validation loss keeps the epoch-12 model while you try stronger regularization.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: HNSW layers: a skip list made of graphs
question: A teammate sets m_L very high (for example 5) so the hierarchy is taller. What does the HNSW paper say happens when m_L is too large?
options: Recall drops to zero because layer 0 becomes empty
Memory shrinks because fewer links are stored
Neighbors overlap more across layers, so extra layers add little and search gets slower
Nothing changes; m_L only affects build time
explain: The paper explains that larger m_L means more overlap between layers (more nodes repeated on many layers), which hurts performance, while too small m_L increases the number of hops on each layer. That tradeoff is why it picks m_L = 1/ln M, matching a skip list with p = 1/M.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Version ranges and lockfiles: why new code arrives unasked
question: Which statement about lockfiles is correct?
options: A lockfile only records direct dependencies
A lockfile makes ranges in package.json irrelevant for npm update
A lockfile freezes the whole tree and checks each tarball's hash, so new releases only enter when someone deliberately updates it
A lockfile stops a malicious version from ever being installed, even when you update
explain: It pins every node, direct and transitive, and stores an integrity hash. It does not judge whether a version is safe: if you update during an attack, the lockfile faithfully records the bad version.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Protestware: when the legitimate maintainer is the threat
question: Which control would NOT have flagged colors 1.4.1 as suspicious?
options: Verifying the package's registry signature
Waiting seven days before adopting new versions
Noticing a test process stuck at 100 percent CPU
Reading the diff between 1.4.0 and 1.4.1
explain: The signature was valid: the real maintainer published it. Diff review, cooldowns and behaviour monitoring all look at what the code does or how the community reacts, which is where a producer attack shows.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Signing artifacts: from long-lived keys to Sigstore
question: A team verifies container images with cosign but sets `--certificate-identity-regexp='.*'` and `--certificate-oidc-issuer-regexp='.*'`. What does a passing check now prove?
options: Only that someone, anyone, with any OIDC identity signed it and logged the signature
That the image has no vulnerabilities
Nothing, because cosign rejects wildcard flags
That the image was built by the team's release workflow
explain: Wildcards accept every identity, including an attacker's. Sigstore's quickstart uses them only to demonstrate; real policies name the exact signer.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: xz-utils I: two years of patient social engineering
question: Why did the 'Jigar Kumar' and 'Dennis Ens' emails matter to the attack?
options: They hacked Lasse Collin's account
They contained malicious patches
They pressured an overworked maintainer to hand more control to Jia Tan
They reported bugs that Jia Tan then fixed
explain: They wrote complaints about slow progress and urged a new maintainer. Shortly after, Lasse Collin described Jia Tan as practically a co-maintainer and gave commit access.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: The Gaussian loop: unbiased fits that still shrink to a point
question: Which statement about the M = 10 loop is correct?
options: The expected variance falls each generation, so the estimator is biased
The typical variance stays near 1, but the expected variance collapses
The expected variance stays at 1, but the typical (median) run collapses toward 0
Both the expected and typical variance stay near 1
explain: Unbiasedness makes the variance a martingale, so its expectation is 1 forever. The median follows the drift of the log and collapses. A heavy right tail of rare runs keeps the mean at 1.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Using synthetic data well: filter, diversify, anchor
question: Which change most directly addresses the failure that phi-1's authors warned about when prompting a model to write textbooks?
options: Lower the sampling temperature for cleaner text
Generate ten times more textbooks from the same prompt
Vary the topic and target audience in each generation prompt
Train the student for more epochs on the synthetic set
explain: Their concern was homogeneous, redundant output: a generator repeats its most probable content. Constraining topics and audiences forces coverage. Lower temperature and more samples from one prompt make redundancy worse.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: mmap: putting a file into your address space
question: You want to map a file starting at byte 5000. Page size is 4096. What do you pass, and where is byte 5000 in the result?
options: offset 5000; byte 5000 is at p[0]
offset 0; byte 5000 is at p[904]
offset 8192; byte 5000 is at p[-3192]
offset 4096; byte 5000 is at p[904]
explain: offset must be page-aligned, so round 5000 down to 4096 and add the remainder yourself: 5000 - 4096 = 904. Passing 5000 fails with EINVAL. Remember to extend length by the same 904 bytes so the end of the range you want is still covered.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: Watching and restricting system calls: strace, faults and seccomp
question: A sandbox's seccomp allow-list includes SYS_open, SYS_read, SYS_write and SYS_exit_group. A program inside calls fopen("data.txt", "r") and gets EPERM. Why?
options: fopen needs SYS_close on the list before it can open
glibc's open wrapper has used the openat system call since glibc 2.26, and openat is not on the list
Filters cannot allow file system calls
fopen is served by the vDSO
explain: seccomp filters match the system call number the kernel sees, and seccomp(2) notes that glibc switched open to openat in 2.26. Strace the program to find the calls it really makes, then build the list from that.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Measuring correctly: intended start times and HdrHistogram
question: You can only sample a queue's latency once every 100 ms from a monitoring thread that blocks while sampling. One sample reads 1,050 ms. With recordValueWithExpectedInterval(1050, 100), how many values are recorded in total?
explain: It records 1050, then 950, 850, ..., 150: the loop continues while the value is at least 100, so it stops before 50. That is 1 + 9 = 10 values.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Merging overlapping roles: union, gaps and double counting
question: Roles are stored with *inclusive* end months, and the merge test is `s <= end`. One job ends in Mar 2019 and the next starts in Apr 2019. What happens?
options: They merge correctly
A spurious gap of length 0 is recorded between them, because Apr is greater than Mar
The second job is dropped
The total is 1 month too high
explain: With inclusive ends, back-to-back jobs differ by one, so `s <= end` fails and the code records a gap from Mar to Apr that contains no months. Totals still add up, but gap reports and gap filters break. Half-open intervals avoid the off-by-one entirely.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Coverage: how pass@k grows with the number of samples
question: Brown et al. find coverage on many tasks grows roughly log-linearly with k over several orders of magnitude. What best explains that shape?
options: Samples from an LLM become more accurate as you draw more of them
The benchmark mixes problems whose per-sample success rates span many orders of magnitude, so each 10x in k unlocks another slice
Temperature is raised automatically as k grows
pass@k for a single problem is linear in log k
explain: For one problem, pass@k is a sharp S-curve in log k. Averaging many such curves with offsets spread across decades smooths them into a steady rise. Samples are independent and do not get better individually.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Thinking longer: reasoning models and budget forcing
question: You fine-tuned a model like s1 and force 10 extra "Wait" continuations on every hard problem. Accuracy drops compared with 4. What is the most likely cause?
options: The model forgot its fine-tuning
Too many suppressed stops push it into repetitive loops or past the context window, so extra tokens stop adding useful reasoning
Appending "Wait" changes the model's weights
Budget forcing only works on easy problems
explain: s1 reports that scaling with budget forcing flattens and that suppressing the end-of-thinking delimiter too often leads to repetitive loops, while the context window bounds total length.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: A hidden state that is itself a model you train while reading
question: Why does a TTT layer have constant cost per token while softmax attention does not?
options: Its weights W have a fixed size no matter how many tokens were absorbed, while attention's KV list grows by one entry per token and must be scanned
TTT skips tokens with small gradients, so it processes fewer tokens
TTT uses a sliding window over the last 16 tokens
Attention recomputes the whole prefix from scratch for each new token
explain: The cost of an update or read depends on the state size. W stays the same shape forever, so each step costs the same; attention's state is the KV cache, which grows linearly, so reading it costs O(t). Attention does not recompute the prefix (the cache prevents that).

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Titans: surprise, momentum and a forget gate for neural memory
question: Why does Titans take every gradient in a chunk at the chunk-start memory before running the momentum scan, instead of scanning the exact token-by-token rule?
options: The scan only works on scalars, and fixing the memory makes it scalar
In the exact rule each gradient depends on the memory just written, so the inputs to the recurrence are not known in advance; fixing them at M_0 turns it into a linear recurrence with known inputs
Momentum is undefined inside a chunk, so it must be switched off there
Taking gradients at M_0 makes the result identical to the exact rule
explain: A scan needs a linear recurrence whose inputs are already known. The exact gradient at token t needs M_(t-1), which depends on all earlier updates, so it is not. The chunk approximation, the same one TTT's mini-batches make, computes all u_t at M_0 in parallel. It changes the result, which is why chunk size is a quality knob.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: After Titans: better objectives, optimal solvers, and replication
question: What did the Titans Revisited reimplementation conclude?
options: Titans' published numbers reproduced exactly on the original benchmarks
The full model did not always beat baselines, mostly because of chunking, but the neural memory consistently helped over attention-only variants
The neural memory never helped, so the gains came from persistent tokens
MAG was best on every task they tried
explain: Their reimplementation, run mostly on different tasks, found chunking was the main source of degradation, the memory helped consistently, and persistent tokens alone did little. They focused on MAC, so they make no claim about MAG versus the other variants.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Sizing M, filling the depot, and the memory you pay
question: Over the last interval a cache's depot held between 120 and 128 full magazines. Using the paper's working-set rule, how many could be reclaimed if memory runs low?
options: 0, magazines are never reclaimed
explain: The working set is the variation, 128 minus 120 = 8 magazines. The 120 magazines that were never touched during the interval are eligible for reclaiming, just as in the paper's 37 to 47 example where 37 are reclaimable.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: PEAK and TaHiTI: from backlog to handover
question: A team routinely runs hunt procedures it downloaded from public repositories, but has not yet written its own. Which HMM level?
options: HMM2 Procedural
HMM1 Minimal
HMM0 Initial
HMM4 Leading
explain: Bianco's HMM2 describes teams that can follow procedures developed by others but do not yet create new ones (HMM3). HMM1 teams mainly search for indicators from reports; HMM4 teams automate their own successful hunts.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: An intelligence-driven hunt: living off the land and Volt Typhoon
question: Why does an indicator-based search (hashes of malicious files) find little in a Volt Typhoon intrusion?
options: The group mainly uses signed tools already present on Windows with valid accounts, so there are few attacker files to hash
Volt Typhoon encrypts all its files
Hash searches only work on Linux
The advisories publish no indicators at all
explain: Living off the land means ntdsutil, wmic, netsh and PowerShell: Microsoft's own signed binaries, identical on every machine. Their hashes are the same for the admin and the attacker. The advisories do publish some indicators (for example of proxy tools), but the core activity has to be found by behaviour and baseline.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Measuring a hunt programme, and where to practise
question: Which metric does PEAK call the most obvious measure of a hunting team, but not a strong indicator of success?
options: Gaps identified and closed
Unique ATT&CK techniques hunted
Detections created or updated
Number of incidents found during hunts
explain: Bianco calls incidents found the most obvious measure but 'not a strong indicator of success', because hunters do not control whether an adversary is present or active. The other three measure lasting improvements the team does control.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Strategic, operational, tactical and technical intelligence
question: Why did Mandiant expect the APT1 indicators to lose value faster than the report's strategic conclusions?
options: Because MD5 hashes expire after a year
Because strategic intelligence is classified and indicators are not
Because publishing indicators tells the adversary exactly what to change, and infrastructure and files are cheap to change
Because indicators are always wrong
explain: The report says publishing indicators 'dramatically shortens their lifespan' and expected the unit to change techniques. Domains, IPs and hashes sit low on the Pyramid of Pain, so they are cheap to replace; the organisation's mission and sponsor do not change because a report was published.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Kill chain and ATT&CK as analytic frames
question: An adversary uses a new zero-day exploit but the same command-and-control domains and the same mail-theft tool as last year. According to the kill chain paper, what does that mean for a well-prepared defender?
options: Nothing can stop a zero-day, so the intrusion succeeds
The defender must first attribute the zero-day to a country
Mitigations for the repeated indicators in other phases can still break the chain
Only patching can help
explain: The paper argues the exploit 'is but one change in a broader process': if intruders reuse tools or infrastructure in other phases, defenders holding mitigations for those indicators still stop the intrusion. That is the value of complete, multi-phase coverage.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Attribution: levels, evidence and its limits
question: Two intrusions share HTRAN, Mimikatz (a widely used credential theft tool) and Cobalt Strike. A junior analyst wants to merge them into one cluster. What is the best response?
options: Merge them: three shared tools is strong evidence
Merge them and attribute the cluster to China because HTRAN was in the APT1 report
Do not merge on these alone: all three are widely used, so they have low uniqueness; look for rare shared features such as custom code or infrastructure registration details
Never cluster intrusions without a government statement
explain: Mandiant's APT1 appendix warns that widely available tools are not useful by themselves as indicators of a specific group; rare features such as a custom backdoor carry far more weight, and even those are rarely enough alone.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Assets and adversaries: what is worth taking, and by whom
question: Why should a threat model list a support engineer's login as an asset, even though it holds no data itself?
options: Because logins are covered by compliance rules
Because it is a stepping stone that grants access to data the attacker wants
Because support engineers are the most likely attackers
Because every account must be listed for completeness
explain: Access is an asset. A login that can read any user's notes is as valuable to an attacker as the notes themselves. Compliance and completeness are not the reason, and the model makes no claim that support staff are likely attackers.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Attack trees: start from the attacker's goal
question: An AND node has children costing 300 and 700. It sits under an OR node whose other child costs 800. What is the OR node's cost?
explain: The AND node sums: 300 + 700 = 1,000. The OR node takes the cheaper of 1,000 and 800, which is 800.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Case: Target 2013, a vendor login across a trust boundary
question: Which single change would most directly have broken the Target attack path at the start?
options: Encrypting the card database at rest
Faster antivirus updates on POS terminals
Restricting the vendor login so it could reach only the billing system, not the internal network
Requiring Target employees to change passwords monthly
explain: The vendor credential was the first link, and its access beyond billing let the attackers move inward. Encryption at rest would not stop RAM scraping, which reads data in memory; employee password rotation was not the entry point.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: Why memory is becoming a hierarchy of tiers
question: Using the model with DRAM 100 ns and CXL 200 ns, what fraction of accesses must hit DRAM to get an average of 120 ns?
explain: 120 = 100h + 200(1 minus h) = 200 minus 100h, so h = 0.8. Each 1% of accesses moved to CXL adds 1 ns here.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Splitting a series into trend, season and remainder
question: A city's electricity demand used to peak in winter (heating) and now peaks in summer (air conditioning). Which decomposition choice handles this best?
options: Classical decomposition, because it averages each month over all years
A larger moving-average window for the trend
STL with a seasonal component allowed to change over time
Multiplicative classical decomposition
explain: Classical decomposition assumes the same seasonal pattern every year, so it would average the old winter peak with the new summer peak. STL lets the seasonal component evolve, which is exactly what this series needs. FPP3 uses this electricity example to illustrate the limitation.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: What TLS promises, and what it does not
question: Which attacker does TLS assume?
options: Only a passive eavesdropper who records traffic
An attacker with malware on the client machine
An attacker who controls the server
An active network attacker who can read, drop, modify, replay and inject packets
explain: TLS is designed for a fully active attacker on the network path. Malware on an endpoint or a compromised server is outside its threat model, because those see the data before encryption or after decryption.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: TLS 1.2, RSA key exchange and forward secrecy
question: Why does ECDHE give forward secrecy while the server still has a long-term certificate key?
options: The long-term key only signs; session keys come from ephemeral DH values deleted after use, so the long-term key never decrypts anything
The certificate key is rotated every connection
ECDHE uses a longer key
The certificate is encrypted
explain: Forward secrecy comes from separating the roles: signing proves identity, ephemeral DH creates the secret. A stolen signing key lets you forge future handshakes but cannot recompute past DH secrets.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Hostname checks and the code that turns verification off
question: Why is `check_hostname = False` dangerous even when the chain is still verified (CERT_REQUIRED)?
options: It disables encryption
Any valid certificate for any domain, which an attacker can get for their own domain in minutes, would be accepted for this host
It makes the handshake slower
It turns off forward secrecy
explain: Chain validation proves a CA vouched for some name. Without the hostname check, the attacker simply presents a genuine certificate for a domain they own.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Revocation: CRL, OCSP, stapling, and why short-lived certs won
question: A company's server key leaks. Its certificate has 300 days left. Which plan actually limits the damage most?
options: Revoke the certificate and keep using the same key with a new certificate
Do nothing until expiry
Revoke the certificate, generate a new key pair, get a new certificate, and move to automated short-lived certificates
Turn on OCSP stapling
explain: A new certificate on the old key is still usable by the thief. Revocation helps where clients check CRLs, but short lifetimes bound the exposure regardless of how clients check.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: goto fail: one duplicated line that skipped the signature check
question: Which change, applied alone, would have prevented this bug from shipping?
options: A test that connects to a server signing its key exchange with the wrong key and expects the handshake to fail
Switching from SHA-1 to SHA-256
Using longer RSA keys
Enabling OCSP
explain: The code passed every test with valid servers because valid signatures and skipped checks look the same. Only a negative test (bad input must be rejected) exposes a check that never runs.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Fused softmax: one row per program, reductions on chip
question: Why does the fused softmax kernel move about 4x fewer bytes than the five-op PyTorch version?
options: Triton compresses data before writing it to DRAM
Intermediates (max, shifted values, exponentials, sums) stay in registers instead of round-tripping through DRAM
Triton uses fp16 automatically
The fused kernel skips the max subtraction
explain: Each separate op reads its input from DRAM and writes its output back. Fusing keeps all intermediates on chip, leaving one read and one write of the matrix: 2MN instead of 8MN + 4M elements.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Everything is a token: Chameleon and Emu3
question: A product team wants a Chameleon-style model to read dense receipts and screenshots. What is the main risk the Chameleon paper itself points to?
options: Next-token prediction cannot model 2D layouts at all
The model cannot attend from text to image tokens
The vocabulary has no room for more image codes
The discrete tokenizer reconstructs text-heavy images poorly, which upper-bounds OCR quality
explain: With 13 bits per token and 1024 tokens per 512 px image, fine glyph detail is the first thing lost. The paper calls this a core weakness that bounds OCR-heavy tasks. Separate understanding encoders (lesson 5) are one answer.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: One app, two isolation layers: why a whole OS is redundant
question: Why did library operating systems from the 1990s, such as Exokernel, never see wide deployment, while unikernels can run on public clouds?
options: Their libraries were written in unsafe languages
They had to support many kinds of real hardware; a hypervisor exposes a few standard virtual devices instead
They required multicore CPUs that did not exist yet
Hypervisors run library OSes faster than bare metal does
explain: The Mirage paper's argument: libOSes struggled with real-world hardware support. A hypervisor's virtual devices (netfront, blkfront, virtio) are a small, stable target, so only a few simple drivers are needed.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Paravirtual I/O up close: one packet through a virtqueue
question: With VIRTIO_F_EVENT_IDX negotiated, the device has set avail_event = 5. The driver adds buffers one at a time, taking the available ring's idx from 3 up to 7. After which addition must it notify?
options: After every addition, since notifications are never optional
When idx becomes 5
When idx goes from 5 to 6: the entry was placed at index 5
Never, because event indices replace notifications
explain: The spec says the driver must notify when the idx that determined where the new entry went equals avail_event, that is when idx reaches avail_event + 1 = 6. Other additions should not notify.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: The spectrum: Linux-based unikernels, microVMs and sandboxes
question: On UKL, Redis linked unmodified into the kernel gained only modestly, but after it was changed to call internal kernel routines directly (a custom path inside the kernel) it gained 26% throughput. Given Lupine's finding, where did most of that 26% come from?
options: From removing the user/kernel mode switch, which the unmodified build still paid
From running on bare metal instead of in a VM
From skipping the general system call path and its generic layers, a specialization of the work done per request
From UKL's multi-core support
explain: The unmodified UKL build already runs at supervisor privilege, so the crossing is gone and the gain is modest, as Lupine found with KML.
